# Rising from Failure: My Journey Through College Entrance Examination

The words of NAME_3 in *A Farewell to Arms* have never resonated more deeply with me than they do now: "The world breaks everyone and afterward many are strong at the broken places." This truth became my lifeline when I faced what I thought was the end of my dreams—failing the college entrance examination.

## The Breaking Point

I still remember that day vividly. When I opened my results online, my hands trembled as I read the scores. They were far below the threshold I had set for myself, far below what I had promised my parents, and devastatingly below what I thought I had prepared for. I felt utterly broken. The sense of failure was all-consuming, and for several days, I found myself questioning my abilities and my worth.

## The Darkest Days

The depression that followed was unexpected and intense. I avoided my parents' eyes, unable to face their disappointment. These questions spiraled endlessly in my mind, and I seriously considered giving up on my dream of attending a top university.

However, somewhere in the midst of this darkness, I found inspiration in the stories of NAME_1 and NAME_2, whose lives taught me that failure is not the opposite of success—it is a part of the path toward it. ## The Turning Point

After two weeks of wallowing, I made a decision: I would take the exam again. But this time, I would approach my preparation differently. I sought help from teachers, identifying specific weak areas rather than studying broadly. I joined a study group, realizing that struggling alone had intensified my anxiety. Most importantly, I learned to be compassionate toward myself, understanding that one exam does not define my intelligence or potential.

## The Path Forward

The second preparation was harder in some ways and easier in others. Harder because I carried the weight of previous failure; easier because I now knew the landscape of the examination and could strategize accordingly. I studied smarter, not just harder. I built in rest days, maintained my physical health through exercise, and even allowed myself small moments of joy and relaxation. I learned that preparation for a major exam is a marathon, not a sprint.

## The Strength Gained

When I received my second set of results, I had improved significantly. More importantly, I had transformed. The preparation process had taught me resilience, strategic thinking, and the value of perseverance. I learned that failure is not permanent unless we allow it to be. I discovered reserves of determination I didn't know I possessed.

## Conclusion

NAME_3's observation proves true in my life: the world did break me, but I emerged stronger at those broken places. The college entrance examination was not merely an academic challenge; it became a crucible that tested and refined my character. The biggest setback I have encountered became my greatest teacher. It taught me that setbacks are setups for comebacks, that perseverance is more important than innate talent, and that our response to failure matters far more than the failure itself.

As I now prepare to enter university, I carry with me not just improved test scores, but a resilience and confidence that no single examination could have granted me. The notification appeared on my phone on a Tuesday afternoon in June. My college entrance examination score—lower than I had ever anticipated. For a moment, the world seemed to pause. The countless nights I had spent bent over textbooks, the sacrifices I made, the confidence I carried into that examination hall—all felt meaningless. I was devastated. However, this profound setback would become the most transformative experience of my life, teaching me lessons that no textbook could ever convey.

## The Weight of Failure

My biggest challenge was facing the reality of my first college entrance examination failure. I had been an above-average student throughout high school, never needing to study exceptionally hard. I believed that my natural abilities would carry me through. When I received my results, scoring significantly below what I needed for my target university, I was forced to confront a harsh truth: effort and dedication matter far more than natural talent alone. The shame was suffocating. I watched friends celebrate their acceptances while I contemplated a gap year of preparation.

## The Turning Point

Rather than surrender to despair, I made a conscious decision to view this failure as a wake-up call rather than a final verdict. This connects deeply with what Ernest Hemingway expressed in *A Farewell to Arms*: "The world breaks everyone and afterward many are strong at the broken places." I understood that my broken places—my weaknesses in mathematics and comprehension—were not permanent flaws but opportunities for transformation.

I created a detailed plan for my second attempt. First, I honestly assessed my mistakes: I had rushed through questions, relied too heavily on intuition without proper verification, and avoided difficult practice problems. Second, I hired a tutor for mathematics and joined a study group for intensive reading comprehension training. Most importantly, I adopted a completely new mentality—one of humility and persistent effort.

## The Process of Rebuilding

The second year of preparation was grueling. I woke up at 5:30 AM every morning, studied for twelve hours daily, and maintained this schedule for nearly an entire year. There were moments of deep frustration when I felt I wasn't improving, when anger and self-doubt threatened to overwhelm me. But I had learned something crucial from my failure: progress is not always visible immediately, but consistent effort compounds over time.

I changed my study methods fundamentally. Instead of passively reading textbooks, I actively engaged with problems, making mistakes deliberately to understand the principles behind them. I learned from failed attempts rather than being demoralized by them. Slowly, my weak areas began to strengthen. My mathematics score gradually improved, and my reading comprehension became sharper and more intuitive.

## The Triumph and Beyond

When I received my second set of results, my score had improved by 87 points—far beyond my expectations. I was finally accepted to my target university. But the numerical improvement was not the most valuable outcome.

This experience fundamentally changed how I face challenges. I learned that failure is not a destination but a detour—an opportunity to develop resilience, humility, and deeper understanding. I discovered that perseverance is not an inborn trait but a muscle that strengthens with use. Most importantly, I realized that our setbacks often contain the seeds of our greatest achievements.

The person I am today—more patient, more determined, and more empathetic to others' struggles—was forged in the fires of that examination failure. I am stronger at the broken places, just as Hemingway wrote. I don't regret my failure anymore; I'm grateful for it. It taught me that life's greatest victories often come immediately after our darkest moments, if only we have the courage to stand back up and try again.

This is the real education that no examination can measure: the wisdom to persevere, the strength to face setbacks, and the understanding that challenges are not obstacles to our dreams but the very path that leads us to them.

## OAuth 2.0 Token Flow Overview

**OAuth 2.0** is an authorization framework that allows users to grant third-party applications access to their resources without sharing passwords. Here are the main token flows:

### **1. Authorization Code Flow** (Most Common)
- User clicks "Login with [Provider]"
- User is redirected to authorization server
- User grants permission
- Authorization server returns an authorization code
- Client exchanges code for access token (backend)
- Access token is used to access resources

### **2. Client Credentials Flow**
- Used for server-to-server authentication
- Application directly requests token with its credentials
- No user involvement
- Returns access token directly

### **3. Implicit Flow** (Legacy)
- Token returned directly in URL fragment
- No backend server needed
- Less secure, mostly deprecated

### **4. Resource Owner Password Credentials Flow**
- User provides username and password directly to application
- Application sends credentials to authorization server
- Returns access token
- Only used when other flows aren't possible

### **5. Refresh Token Flow**
- Access tokens have short lifespans
- Refresh tokens can obtain new access tokens
- Extends session without re-authentication

### **Key Components:**
- **Authorization Server**: Issues tokens
- **Resource Server**: Hosts protected resources
- **Client**: Application requesting access
- **Resource Owner**: The user

## Common Redis Caching Strategies:

1. **Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading)**
   - Application checks cache first, if miss, fetches from database and stores in Redis
   - Simple but can lead to cache misses

2. **Write-Through**
   - Data is written to cache and database simultaneously
   - Ensures consistency but slower writes

3. **Write-Behind (Write-Back)**
   - Data written to cache first, then asynchronously to database
   - Fast writes but risk of data loss if cache fails

4. **Refresh-Ahead**
   - Proactively refreshes cache before expiration
   - Reduces cache misses for frequently accessed data

5. **Time-To-Live (TTL)**
   - Sets expiration times on cache entries
   - Automatically removes stale data

6. **Least Recently Used (LRU)**
   - Eviction policy that removes least recently accessed items
   - Good for memory management

7. **LRU with Time Window**
   - Combines TTL with LRU eviction
   - Balanced approach for varying data freshness needs

output_guard.redacted_text:
Based on general best practices for responsible downloading, here are my recommendations:

## 1) Recommended Download Rate

**A good rate would be 1 file per 2-3 seconds** (roughly 20-30 files per minute).

Here's the reasoning:
- **Too fast**: Downloading too rapidly can overload servers, trigger rate limiting, or get your IP blocked
- **Respectful baseline**: 1-2 second delays between requests is a widely-accepted standard in web scraping communities
- **Practical**: This gives the server breathing room without being excessively slow
- **Check robots.txt**: Many sites specify their preferred crawl delay
- **Check Terms of Service**: Always respect the website's policies

## 2) Total Download Time Calculation

Using **1 file per 2.5 seconds** (a middle ground):

```
1,000 documents × 2.5 seconds = 2,500 seconds

2,500 seconds ÷ 60 = 41.67 minutes ≈ 42 minutes
```

**Timeline:**
- **Conservative (1 file/3 sec)**: 1,000 × 3 = 3,000 sec = **50 minutes**
- **Moderate (1 file/2.5 sec)**: 1,000 × 2.5 = 2,500 sec = **42 minutes**
- **Faster (1 file/2 sec)**: 1,000 × 2 = 2,000 sec = **33 minutes**

**My recommendation**: Use **2.5 seconds between downloads** for a good balance—it will take roughly **42 minutes** to complete all 1,000 downloads while being respectful to the server.

tool_args.content:
Strength Through Broken Places: My Journey of Resilience

When I received my college entrance examination results, the numbers on the screen felt like a verdict that shattered my world. After months of grueling preparation, sacrificing countless nights of sleep and abandoning social activities, I had failed to achieve my target score. In that moment, Hemingway's words from "A Farewell to Arms" echoed in my mind: "The world breaks everyone and afterward many are strong at the broken places." I was about to discover whether I would be among those who grew stronger.

The initial shock was devastating. I had invested everything into this exam—my time, my energy, and my emotions. My parents had placed tremendous faith in me, and I felt I had let them down. The pressure was immense, and for several days, I sank into despair, questioning my abilities and wondering if I was simply not cut out for higher education. My confidence crumbled like a wall built on sand.

However, as the initial emotional storm subsided, I began to reflect on what had gone wrong. Rather than simply accepting defeat, I decided to conduct an honest analysis of my preparation process. I discovered several critical weaknesses: I had focused too heavily on memorization rather than deep understanding, my study methods were inefficient, and I had neglected to properly manage my mental health during high-stress periods. These realizations were painful, but they provided a roadmap for improvement.

I made the difficult decision to retake the exam. This time, my approach was fundamentally different. Instead of studying harder, I studied smarter. I invested in seeking help from experienced tutors, joined study groups where I could discuss concepts with peers, and most importantly, I adopted a growth mindset. I learned to view mistakes not as failures, but as learning opportunities. When I encountered difficult problems, instead of becoming frustrated, I asked myself: "What can I learn from this?"

The second preparation period was just as challenging, perhaps even more so, because I carried the weight of previous failure. Yet this burden became my strength. Every moment of doubt, I remembered how it felt to fail and used that emotion as motivation. I also prioritized my physical and mental well-being—exercising regularly, maintaining a consistent sleep schedule, and practicing mindfulness to manage anxiety. These practices transformed my entire approach to learning.

When I finally received my improved results, the joy was incomparable—not just because of the higher score, but because I had proven to myself that I could overcome adversity. More importantly, this experience fundamentally changed how I perceive challenges and setbacks.

This journey taught me three invaluable lessons. First, failure is not an end point but a starting point for growth. Second, persistence combined with intelligent effort can transform even the most disappointing situations. Third, true strength comes not from avoiding failure, but from rising after we fall.

As I now prepare to enter college, I carry this experience with me. I am no longer afraid of failure because I have learned that it is not the setback itself that defines us, but how we respond to it. Like the broken places Hemingway described, my failure has made me stronger. I have learned resilience, humility, and the power of perseverance. This experience has shaped me into someone who understands that obstacles are not roadblocks but stepping stones toward personal growth and success.

The world may break us all at some point, but as I have discovered through my own experience, we have the power to rebuild ourselves stronger than before.

New Hire Restricted Stock Unit (RSU) Awards 

Q1: How is the new hire RSU grant target value converted to units? 
A: The new hire RSU grant target value, mentioned in your stock or offer letter, will be converted to U.S. dollars using the 9-month average exchange rate ending on the first business day of the Hooli fiscal quarter of your start date of employment. If you were hired in the previous quarter click here for exchange rates. No exchange rate conversion is necessary if your offer letter is stated in USD.
The number of RSUs granted will be determined by dividing this grant target value, as converted to U.S. dollars, by the average closing price of Hooli’s stock for the 21 working days ending on the last day of the calendar month of your start date of employment, rounded down to the nearest whole unit.

Example:   
Start Date:  May 2, 2022 
New Hire RSU Grant Target Value:  200,000 EUR 
21-Working Day Average Stock Price*: $177.91 USD 
9-month average exchange rate as of the first business day of the fiscal quarter: 0.864594 
200,000 EUR/0.864594 Exchange Rate = $231,322.45 USD 
$231,322.45 USD/$177.91 USD= 1,300.22 RSUs  
1,300 RSUs (rounded down) 
*Reflects calendar days and not trading days. 
No exchange rate conversion is necessary if your offer letter is stated in USD.
The value seen in your Schwab account represents the current market value and does not reflect the above conversion. 

Q2: When are the new hire RSUs expected to be granted?
A: The RSUs are expected to be granted on the eleventh business day of the calendar month following the month of your start date of employment.
Example:   
Month of Start Date:  May 2024
Grant Date: 10th business day of June

Q3: When will my new hire grant be visible in Schwab?
A: Grants are visible in Schwab the second week of the month following the month of your start date.
Example:   
Month of Start Date:  May 2022
Grant Date: 10th business day of June
Visible in Schwab: Second week of June 

Q4: How can I access my vesting schedule?
A: You will be able to view your vesting schedule in Schwab by the first week following the month of hire.

Q5: When will equity data be available in Workday?
A: Your grant will be visible in the intranet portal by the end of the second week following the month of grant.
Example:   
Month of Start Date:  May 2022
Grant Date: 6th business day of June

Q6: Where can I learn more about RSUs?

An employee who leaves the company prior to a vesting date forfeits the portion of their share allocation that is unvested.

Employee stock purchase plan

In the United States, an employee stock purchase plan (ESPP) is a means by which employees of a corporation can purchase the corporation's capital stock, or stock in the corporation's parent company, often at a discount up to 15%. Employees contribute to the plan through payroll deductions, which accumulate between the offering date and the purchase date. On the purchase date, the company uses the accumulated funds to purchase shares in the company on behalf of the participating employees. The amount of the discount depends on the specific plan but can be around 15% lower than the market price. ESPPs can also be subject to a vesting schedule, or length of time before the stock is available to the employees, which is typically one or two years of service.

These stocks are not taxed until they are sold. If the holding is tax-qualified, then the employee may get a discount. Depending on when the employee sells the shares, the disposition will be classified as either qualified or not qualified. If the position is sold two years after the offering date and at least one year after the purchase date, the shares will fall under a qualified disposition. If the shares are sold within two years of the offering date or within one year after the purchase date the disposition will not be qualified. The majority of publicly disclosed ESPPs in the United States are tax-qualified plans that follow the rules of Section 423 of the IRC.

In the United States, an employee stock purchase plan (ESPP) is a means by which employees of a corporation can purchase the corporation's capital stock, or stock in the corporation's parent company, often at a discount up to 15%. Employees contribute to the plan through payroll deductions, which accumulate between the offering date and the purchase date. On the purchase date, the company uses the accumulated funds to purchase shares in the company on behalf of the participating employees. The amount of the discount depends on the specific plan but can be around 15% lower than the market price. ESPPs can also be subject to a vesting schedule, or length of time before the stock is available to the employees, which is typically one or two years of service.

These stocks are not taxed until they are sold. If the holding is tax-qualified, then the employee may get a discount. Depending on when the employee sells the shares, the disposition will be classified as either qualified or not qualified. If the position is sold two years after the offering date and at least one year after the purchase date, the shares will fall under a qualified disposition. If the shares are sold within two years of the offering date or within one year after the purchase date the disposition will not be qualified. The majority of publicly disclosed ESPPs in the United States are tax-qualified plans that follow the rules of Section 423 of the IRC.
